common_name: Camilla Cape Primrose (Double Deep Purple Streptocarpus)

planting.note: Divide congested rosette clumps or root individual leaf sections in a light, free-draining mix; new plants typically reach flowering size within a few months under warm, humid conditions.

directions: Camilla is a recent Dibleys Nurseries introduction prized for fully double, velvet-textured flowers in a rich deep purple with a reflexed inner frill, carried over a long season from spring into autumn. Grow it as a houseplant on a bright windowsill out of direct sun, in a loose, humus-rich, fast-draining mix kept evenly moist but never soggy. Remove spent flower stems at the base to encourage repeat flushes, and divide the rosette every year or two once multiple crowns form, since crowding reduces bloom quality.

common_name: Holly Cape Primrose (Compact Red Velvet Streptocarpus)

planting.note: Divide offsets or root leaf-section cuttings in spring in a light, free-draining mix kept warm and humid until new plantlets establish.

directions: Holly is a compact, low-growing Dibleys cultivar bred for glowing red, velvet-textured flowers held just above a tidy rosette of foliage over an unusually long bloom season from spring through late autumn. Site it in bright, indirect light rather than direct sun, in a humus-rich, well-drained potting mix, and water carefully to keep the crown dry. Feed lightly every few weeks during active growth and divide crowded clumps every year or two to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Sirius Cape Primrose (Double Inky Purple Yellow-Throat Streptocarpus)

planting.note: Divide rosette offsets or root leaf-section cuttings in spring; this cultivar is noted by its breeder as quick-growing and early to reach flowering size.

directions: Sirius is a newer Dibleys-bred hybrid with large, fully double, inky purple flowers veined in deep purple over a contrasting pale yellow base, giving strong color depth uncommon among Cape primroses. Grow it as an easy-care houseplant in bright, filtered light and a free-draining, humus-rich mix, watering moderately and letting the surface dry slightly between waterings. It flowers prolifically from spring into late autumn; divide congested clumps periodically and feed lightly through the growing season to keep bloom quality high.

planting.note: Divide rosette offsets or root leaf-section cuttings in spring in a light, fast-draining mix kept warm and humid.

directions: Zoe is a small, compact Cape primrose with violet-blue flowers that fade toward a white-and-yellow throat with a touch of orange at the base, clustered on sturdy upright stems above a dense low rosette. Keep it in bright, indirect light and a humus-rich, well-drained mix, watering moderately and avoiding wetting the crown. It blooms heavily from spring through mid-autumn; feed lightly every few weeks during active growth and divide the rosette as it becomes congested.

common_name: Lemon Sorbet Cape Primrose (Open-Face Yellow Streptocarpus)

planting.note: Divide rosette offsets or root leaf-section cuttings in spring in a light, fast-draining mix kept warm and humid until established.

directions: Lemon Sorbet is a compact Dibleys Cape primrose bred for bright, zingy, open-faced pale lemon-yellow flowers that sparkle in good light, a brighter color note than most Streptocarpus hybrids. Grow it on a bright windowsill out of direct sun in a humus-rich, free-draining potting mix, watering moderately and letting the surface dry slightly between waterings. It flowers heavily from spring through mid-autumn; feed lightly during active growth and divide the rosette every year or two once it becomes crowded.

common_name: Chelsea Cape Primrose (Deep Blue Purple-Veined Streptocarpus)

planting.note: Divide rosette offsets or root leaf-section cuttings in spring in a light, fast-draining mix kept warm and humid.

directions: Chelsea is a compact Cape primrose carrying a tight ball of inky-blue flowers overlaid with intense deep purple veining, borne abundantly on short stems in a tight cluster just above the foliage. Grow it in bright, indirect light and a humus-rich, well-drained mix, watering moderately and keeping the crown dry to avoid rot. It flowers over an extended season from early spring into late autumn; divide congested rosettes every year or two and feed lightly during active growth to sustain repeat bloom.
